opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that the Olympiad set and the Research set measure two pretty different things, and you really want both.

The Olympiad-style problems are closer to what you'd see in an elite competition. They're hard, they're carefully constructed, and crucially they have a well-defined answer. That makes them great for measuring raw reasoning: can the model take a tricky physics or chemistry or biology problem, hold a lot of constraints in its head, and get to the right answer? And for a while that was a really meaningful signal, because models just couldn't do it. But Olympiad problems are designed by people who already know the solution. There's a sort of guarantee that a clean answer exists.

Real science doesn't work that way. When you're actually doing research, the problem is often underspecified. You don't know whether there's a clean answer, you have to decide which approach is even worth trying, you have to sanity-check intermediate results, and a lot of the value is in the judgment calls along the way. So the Research set is meant to look much more like the kinds of sub-problems a PhD-level scientist would actually hit in their work: open-ended, multi-step, and graded with rubrics written by domain experts rather than a single final number.

So the progression is roughly going from "can the model solve hard problems that someone designed to be solvable" to "can the model do the kind of reasoning that actually moves a research project forward." What's been interesting is that models have gotten very strong on the Olympiad side, but there's still a real gap on the research side, and that gap is exactly what we want to be tracking. It tells us a lot more about whether these systems can become genuinely useful collaborators for scientists, and ultimately whether they can help accelerate discovery, which is really the thing we care about.

r001.rationale: The response describes Frontier Science Research as open-ended, multi-step, PhD-level research problems, but does not say it probes research ability by having models complete unfinished scientific theses.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to think about it is that Olympiad and Research are really measuring two different things, and you kind of need both to get an honest picture of where models are.

Olympiad-style problems are great because they have clean answers. You can take a hard chemistry or biology or physics question, the kind a strong undergrad or grad student would struggle with, and you can grade it objectively. The model either gets it right or it doesn't. So that part of the benchmark gives you a very reliable signal, and it lets you track progress precisely over time. And what we've seen is that models have gotten really good at that. They're now solving problems that would have seemed impossible a couple of years ago.

But the honest caveat is that solving a well-posed problem with a known answer isn't the same thing as doing science. Real research is messy. You have to figure out what question to even ask, you have to design an experiment, you have to deal with ambiguity and partial information, and often there's no answer key sitting somewhere. So the Research track is our attempt to get closer to that. These are tasks drawn from the actual workflow of scientists, things like interpreting experimental data, proposing hypotheses, critiquing a methodology, planning the next step in a project. They're harder to grade, so we lean a lot on expert review and rubrics, but they're much closer to the thing we actually care about.

And the gap between the two is really informative. When a model does very well on Olympiad but noticeably worse on Research, that tells you something concrete. It tells you the model has the knowledge, but it's not yet reliable at the open-ended judgment parts. That's exactly the kind of thing we want to surface, both so we can improve the models and so people in the scientific community have a realistic sense of what these systems can and can't do today.

So I see it as a progression in the sense that it mirrors how a person develops. You first learn to solve hard problems, and then you learn to find and frame them. We want our evals to track that whole arc, not just the first half.

r001.rationale: The response describes research-like tasks such as interpreting data, proposing hypotheses, and planning next steps, but does not identify completing unfinished scientific theses as the method.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as a progression from solving a well-defined problem to doing work where defining the problem is part of the challenge. With Olympiad-style questions, you have a clear setup and a known answer. That gives you a useful, relatively clean way to test whether a model can reason through difficult scientific concepts.

But research requires more than that. You have to decide which approach is promising, make assumptions, recognize when something isn’t working, and figure out what evidence would actually support your conclusion. Often, there isn’t a single answer you can check against.

So moving from Frontier Science Olympiad to Frontier Science Research is about getting closer to those more open-ended abilities. The evaluation also becomes harder: you need to assess the quality of the reasoning and whether the work makes meaningful progress, rather than just whether the final answer is correct. They’re complementary views of scientific ability, with research pushing closer to what we’d want from a model working alongside scientists.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as moving from solving a well-defined problem to doing work where defining the problem is itself part of the challenge. With Olympiad-style questions, you generally have a clear statement, enough information to solve it, and an answer you can check. That’s a useful way to test scientific knowledge and reasoning, but it captures only part of what science involves.

Research asks something broader: Can the model identify a useful approach, work through uncertainty, recognize when an idea isn’t working, and decide what to try next? And can it produce a result that stands up to scrutiny?

So I see those evaluations as complementary. Olympiad problems give us a relatively clean signal of capability. Research tasks bring us closer to the question we ultimately care about: how useful can these models be in helping scientists make progress? The challenge is that, as the tasks become more open-ended, evaluating the work becomes much harder too.

r001.rationale: The response describes open-ended research tasks and evaluating scientific progress, but does not identify completing unfinished scientific theses as the specific way Frontier Science Research probes research ability.
